## Authors’ thesis

The book presents economics as a disciplined way of reasoning about choice under scarcity rather than as a catalogue of predetermined policy answers. Its foundational definition is:

> “Economics is the study of how humans make decisions in the face of scarcity.”
> [V] (Ch. 1, §1.1)

[AP] Scarcity makes tradeoffs unavoidable for individuals, firms, governments, and societies. The economic method therefore asks what is forgone, how incentives alter behaviour, how marginal benefits compare with marginal costs, and how institutions coordinate dispersed decisions. Models such as budget constraints, production possibilities frontiers, demand and supply, utility analysis, firm cost curves, aggregate demand and aggregate supply, and national accounting identities simplify reality so that causal relationships can be examined explicitly (Chs. 1–3, 6–8, 19, 23–26).

[V] “A fundamental principle of economics is that every choice has an opportunity cost.” (Ch. 2, §2.1). [AP] This principle extends from personal consumption to production, environmental protection, public budgets, financial investment, international specialisation, and macroeconomic stabilisation. Policies may shift who receives benefits and bears costs, but they do not abolish scarcity or opportunity cost (Chs. 2, 12, 15, 17, 30–34).

[AP] Markets are treated as powerful information-and-coordination mechanisms, not as universally sufficient institutions. Competitive prices can direct resources towards higher-valued uses, yet market power, externalities, public goods, imperfect information, discrimination, macroeconomic instability, and collective-action problems can separate private incentives from social outcomes. Government action can sometimes narrow these gaps, but it is itself constrained by information, implementation lags, political incentives, regulatory capture, and unintended effects (Chs. 3–4, 8–18, 25, 28, 30–31).

[AP] The macroeconomic argument combines measurement with competing time horizons. GDP, unemployment, inflation, trade balances, productivity, and financial flows describe different dimensions of performance; no one statistic is a complete welfare measure. Keynesian analysis emphasises demand shortfalls, sticky prices and wages, and short-run stabilisation, while neoclassical analysis emphasises flexible adjustment, potential output, productivity, and long-run growth. The text treats these perspectives as complementary over different horizons rather than requiring an exclusive choice between them (Chs. 19–26).

[AP] International economics extends the same method beyond national borders. Comparative advantage explains mutual gains even when productivity is unequal; exchange rates coordinate currencies and financial flows; and protection redistributes income while usually imposing broader efficiency losses. The text nonetheless recognises adjustment costs, strategic concerns, environmental effects, labour standards, and the political durability of concentrated benefits (Chs. 23, 29, 31–34).

## Part I: What Is Economics?

### Chapter 1 — Welcome to Economics!

[AP] Economics begins with scarcity: human wants exceed the goods, services, time, labour, tools, land, and raw materials available to satisfy them. Because even time is finite, every person and society must choose. Division of labour and specialisation can increase production by allowing workers and organisations to concentrate on particular tasks, develop expertise, and exploit differences in productive capacity (Ch. 1, §1.1).

[AP] Microeconomics studies the decisions and interactions of individuals, households, firms, and particular markets; macroeconomics studies economy-wide outcomes such as growth, unemployment, inflation, and trade. The two levels interact: aggregate outcomes emerge from decentralised choices, while national conditions alter the constraints facing those choices (Ch. 1, §1.2).

[AP] Economic theories and models deliberately omit detail to isolate relationships. The circular-flow diagram distinguishes product markets from factor markets and traces exchanges among households and firms. A model is useful insofar as its assumptions and predictions illuminate the question at hand; it is not a literal reproduction of reality (Ch. 1, §1.3).

[AR][BT] The source quotes John Maynard Keynes describing economics as “a method rather than a doctrine” and a “technique of thinking,” using the attribution to frame economics as an analytical apparatus rather than a body of compulsory conclusions (Ch. 1, §1.3).

[AP] Traditional, command, and market economies organise production and distribution differently, but real economies mix these forms. Property rights, laws, regulation, public services, social norms, and global exchange shape even market-oriented systems; “free market” and “government control” are therefore endpoints for comparison rather than complete descriptions of actual economies (Ch. 1, §1.4).

### Chapter 2 — Choice in a World of Scarcity

[AP] A budget constraint maps what a decision-maker can afford. Its slope records the opportunity-cost ratio between two alternatives, points inside it are attainable but do not exhaust the budget, and points outside it are unattainable at current income and prices. Marginal analysis compares the additional benefit and cost of a small change rather than treating a decision as all-or-nothing (Ch. 2, §2.1).

[AP] Sunk costs have already been incurred and cannot be recovered, so rational forward-looking choices should depend on future benefits and costs. The text distinguishes this prescription from the observation that people often remain influenced by past expenditure (Ch. 2, §2.1).

[AE] The source repeatedly uses two-good constraints—such as combinations of health-care and education spending or personal consumption choices—to show that choosing more of one option requires giving up some of the other. Changes in income move the feasible set, while changes in relative prices rotate it (Ch. 2, §2.1).

[AP] A production possibilities frontier represents an economy’s feasible output combinations. Points on the frontier are productively efficient, points inside it are inefficient, and points outside it are currently unattainable. Increasing opportunity cost gives the frontier its bowed shape; technological progress or additional resources can shift it outward (Ch. 2, §2.2).

[AP] Productive efficiency means producing without avoidable waste, while allocative efficiency means selecting the output mix society prefers. Economics can reveal constraints and tradeoffs, but the source explicitly refuses to derive a society’s normative choice from the PPF alone (Ch. 2, §2.2).

> “The study of economics does not presume to tell a society what choice it should make along its production”
> [V] (Ch. 2, §2.2)

[AP] Positive statements describe or predict what is; normative statements express judgements about what ought to be. The text also defends the economic focus on self-interest and incentives as a useful analytical starting point without claiming that people are wholly selfish or that every valuable activity is bought and sold (Ch. 2, §2.3).

## Part II: Supply and Demand

### Chapter 3 — Demand and Supply

[AP] Demand records how much buyers are willing and able to purchase at different prices, holding other influences constant. The law of demand gives a negative relationship between price and quantity demanded. Supply records sellers’ willingness and ability to produce at different prices, with the law of supply giving a positive relationship between price and quantity supplied (Ch. 3, §3.1).

[AP] Market equilibrium occurs where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied. A price above equilibrium creates excess supply and downward pressure on price; a price below equilibrium creates excess demand and upward pressure. The adjustment process coordinates buyers and sellers without requiring one participant to know the entire market (Ch. 3, §3.1).

> “Remember this: When two lines on a diagram cross, this intersection usually means something.”
> [V] (Ch. 3, §3.1)

[AP] A movement along a curve is caused by a change in the good’s own price. A shift in demand instead reflects income, tastes, population, expectations, or prices of substitutes and complements; a shift in supply reflects input costs, technology, natural conditions, taxes and subsidies, expectations, or the number of sellers (Ch. 3, §3.2).

[AP] The four-step method for comparative statics is: draw the initial equilibrium; identify whether the event shifts demand, supply, or both; determine the direction of each shift; and compare the new equilibrium price and quantity with the old. When both curves shift, the model may determine one outcome while leaving the other ambiguous (Ch. 3, §3.3).

[AP] A binding price ceiling produces a shortage, while a binding price floor produces a surplus. The source’s rent-control and agricultural-support discussions stress that legal prices do not remove the underlying imbalance and may change quality, search costs, allocation methods, or production incentives (Ch. 3, §3.4).

[AP] Consumer surplus, producer surplus, and their sum provide a welfare measure for market exchange. At competitive equilibrium, trades for which willingness to pay exceeds marginal cost occur; binding controls or quantity restrictions can prevent mutually beneficial trades and create deadweight loss (Ch. 3, §3.5).

[AR][BT] The chapter invokes Alfred Marshall’s scissors analogy: asking whether demand or supply determines price is like asking which blade of a pair of scissors cuts paper. The bridge supports the text’s insistence that equilibrium is jointly determined (Ch. 3, §3.5).

### Chapter 4 — Labor and Financial Markets

[AP] Demand and supply apply to labour, where the wage is the price of labour and employment is the quantity exchanged. Labour demand is derived from demand for the output workers help produce. Changes in technology, product demand, worker productivity, education, demographics, and alternative employment can shift the market curves (Ch. 4, §4.1).

[AP] Technological change can complement some forms of labour while substituting for others, helping explain changes in wage inequality. Minimum wages and living-wage rules can raise earnings for workers who retain covered jobs while potentially reducing employment when set above equilibrium; the magnitude depends on market structure and elasticities rather than on the legal rule alone (Ch. 4, §4.1).

[AP] In financial markets, savers supply funds and borrowers demand them; the interest rate is the price paid for using purchasing power over time. Household saving, business investment, government borrowing, risk, expected return, inflation, and international capital flows can shift this market (Ch. 4, §4.2).

[AE] Intertemporal examples compare consumption now with consumption later. A higher interest rate raises the reward for postponing consumption but also changes the income of existing savers and borrowers, so the overall response can combine substitution and income effects (Ch. 4, §4.2).

[AP] Market prices compress and transmit information about scarcity, preferences, costs, and opportunities. Price controls can suppress the signal without removing the condition it communicates; the source’s formulation is effectively that criticising the price alone can amount to blaming the messenger (Ch. 4, §4.3).

## Part III: Fundamentals of Microeconomic Theory

### Chapter 5 — Elasticity

[AP] Elasticity measures how responsive one variable is to a change in another. Price elasticity of demand divides the percentage change in quantity demanded by the percentage change in price; price elasticity of supply does the equivalent for quantity supplied. The midpoint method gives the same percentage calculation regardless of the direction of movement between two points (Ch. 5, §5.1).

[AP] Demand or supply is elastic when the absolute response of quantity exceeds the percentage price change, inelastic when it is smaller, and unit elastic when the changes are proportional. Perfectly elastic and perfectly inelastic curves are limiting cases rather than typical market descriptions (Ch. 5, §§5.1–5.2).

[AP] Demand tends to be more elastic when close substitutes exist, when the good takes a large budget share, when it is a luxury rather than a necessity, and when consumers have more time to adjust. Supply likewise becomes more elastic when producers have spare capacity, mobile inputs, inventories, and sufficient adjustment time (Ch. 5, §5.1).

[AP] Elasticity determines how a price change affects total revenue. With elastic demand, a price increase reduces revenue; with inelastic demand, it increases revenue; with unit elasticity, the two effects offset (Ch. 5, §5.3).

[AE] The chapter’s pricing cases—including entertainment subscriptions, transport, coffee, cigarettes, and oil—show that firms and policymakers need an empirical estimate of responsiveness, not merely the direction of the demand curve (Ch. 5, §5.3).

[AP] Tax incidence depends on relative elasticities rather than on whom the statute instructs to remit the tax. The less elastic side of the market bears more of the burden because it has fewer alternatives (Ch. 5, §5.3).

[AP] Income elasticity distinguishes normal from inferior goods; cross-price elasticity distinguishes substitutes from complements. The same framework can be applied to saving, labour supply, and other relationships in which responsiveness is analytically important (Ch. 5, §5.4).

### Chapter 6 — Consumer Choices

[AP] Traditional consumer theory represents satisfaction as utility. Diminishing marginal utility means that additional units of a good tend to add progressively less utility, while a utility-maximising consumer allocates a limited budget so that marginal utility per dollar is equalised across purchases (Ch. 6, §6.1).

[AP] A change in income shifts purchasing power and changes consumption according to whether goods are normal or inferior. A price change combines a substitution effect—movement towards the relatively cheaper good—with an income effect caused by the change in real purchasing power (Ch. 6, §6.2).

[AE] The chapter’s numerical shopping bundles show why comparing marginal utility alone is insufficient: a consumer must divide marginal utility by price to compare the additional satisfaction obtainable from the last dollar spent on each good (Ch. 6, §6.1).

> “Behavioral economics seeks to enrich our understanding of decision-making by integrating the insights of psychology into economics.”
> [V] (Ch. 6, §6.3)

[AP] Behavioural economics adds predictable departures from the traditional model, including loss aversion, framing, mental accounting, present bias, and sensitivity to default rules. Money is economically fungible, but people may place identical dollars into psychologically distinct accounts and make inconsistent choices across them (Ch. 6, §6.3).

[AP] Nudges alter the choice environment without eliminating options—for example, changing a default enrolment rule. The text presents this framework as an enrichment of rational-choice analysis, not proof that behaviour is random or incapable of systematic study (Ch. 6, §6.3).

### Chapter 7 — Production, Costs, and Industry Structure

[AP] Accounting profit subtracts explicit monetary costs from revenue; economic profit also subtracts implicit opportunity costs, including the owner’s foregone alternatives. A firm can therefore report positive accounting profit while earning zero or negative economic profit (Ch. 7, §7.1).

[AP] Production combines labour, capital, natural resources, and entrepreneurship. In the short run at least one input is fixed, while in the long run all inputs can vary. This distinction concerns adjustability, not a universal number of months or years (Ch. 7, §§7.2, 7.4).

[AP] The law of diminishing marginal product states that, with other inputs fixed, additional units of a variable input eventually add progressively less output. Because production and cost are linked, diminishing marginal product causes marginal cost eventually to rise (Ch. 7, §§7.2–7.3).

[AP] Fixed cost does not change with current output; variable cost does. Average fixed cost falls as output rises, average variable and average total cost reflect per-unit costs, and marginal cost records the cost of one additional unit. Marginal cost crosses average variable and average total cost at their minimum points (Ch. 7, §7.3).

[AP] Long-run average cost can fall through economies of scale, remain flat under constant returns to scale, or rise through diseconomies of scale. Scale economies can arise from specialised labour, technology, purchasing, and organisational advantages; excessive complexity can reverse them (Ch. 7, §7.5).

[AP] Industry location can produce agglomeration economies through shared suppliers, specialised labour pools, infrastructure, and knowledge exchange. Conversely, congestion and high local costs can create disadvantages as clusters expand (Ch. 7, §7.5).

### Chapter 8 — Perfect Competition

[AP] Perfect competition assumes many buyers and sellers, an identical product, easy entry and exit, and firms too small to affect market price. Each firm is a price taker facing a horizontal demand curve at the market price, even though market demand slopes downward (Ch. 8, §8.1).

[AP] A profit-maximising firm produces where marginal revenue equals marginal cost, provided the relevant marginal-cost segment is rising. Under perfect competition, price equals marginal revenue, so the operating rule becomes `P = MR = MC` (Ch. 8, §8.2).

[AP] Profit equals total revenue minus total cost, or `(price − average total cost) × quantity`. A firm earns economic profit when price exceeds average total cost, breaks even when they are equal, and incurs a loss when price is lower (Ch. 8, §8.2).

[AP] In the short run, a loss-making firm continues producing if revenue covers variable cost and contributes something towards fixed cost. It shuts down when price falls below average variable cost. The firm’s short-run supply curve is therefore the portion of marginal cost above average variable cost (Ch. 8, §8.2).

[AP] In the long run, profit attracts entry and loss induces exit, shifting market supply until the representative firm earns zero economic profit. Zero economic profit still includes a normal return covering opportunity costs; it does not mean entrepreneurs receive nothing (Ch. 8, §8.3).

> “In a competitive market, profits are a red cape that incites businesses to charge.”
>
> “Losses are the black thundercloud that causes businesses to flee.”
> [V] (Ch. 8, §8.3)

[AP] The model’s long-run equilibrium is productively efficient because firms produce at minimum average cost and allocatively efficient because price equals marginal cost. The text nevertheless cautions that these conclusions depend on assumptions such as complete cost accounting and the absence of externalities or other market failures (Ch. 8, §8.4).

### Chapter 9 — Monopoly

[AP] A monopoly is the sole seller in a market protected by barriers to entry. Barriers can arise from control of a key resource, legal protections such as patents and copyright, network effects, strategic conduct, or economies of scale that make a single producer the least-cost supplier (Ch. 9, §9.1).

[AP] The monopolist faces the market demand curve. To sell more output it must lower the price, including on units it could otherwise have sold at a higher price, so marginal revenue lies below demand. Profit maximisation still occurs where `MR = MC`, but the price is then read from the demand curve (Ch. 9, §9.2).

[AP] Compared with a competitive market, monopoly generally charges a higher price and supplies a lower quantity. Some mutually beneficial transactions do not occur, creating deadweight loss; the central efficiency objection is restricted output, not high price considered in isolation (Ch. 9, §9.2).

[AP] The source distinguishes monopoly profit from the social role of temporary intellectual-property protection. Patents and copyright can raise prices and restrict present use while offering an incentive to incur the cost and risk of invention or creative production (Ch. 9, §9.1).

[AR][BT] The text invokes John Hicks’s observation that the best monopoly profit may be “a quiet life,” connecting protected market power with weaker pressure to reduce costs or innovate (Ch. 9, §9.2).

### Chapter 10 — Monopolistic Competition and Oligopoly

[AP] Monopolistic competition combines many firms and relatively easy entry with differentiated products. Each firm faces a downward-sloping demand curve because branding, location, quality, service, or perceived differences give it limited pricing power (Ch. 10, §10.1).

[AP] Short-run profit maximisation follows the monopoly rule `MR = MC`; long-run entry shifts each incumbent’s demand inward until economic profit is zero. Unlike perfect competition, the long-run firm typically operates with excess capacity and price above marginal cost (Ch. 10, §10.1).

[AP] Advertising may provide information, signal quality, or strengthen competition, but it may also create artificial differentiation and reinforce market power. The text treats its effects as empirical and context-dependent rather than intrinsically beneficial or wasteful (Ch. 10, §10.1).

[AP] Oligopoly contains a small number of interdependent firms. Each firm’s best action depends on how rivals respond, making strategic behaviour and game theory central. Firms may compete aggressively, coordinate tacitly, or form explicit cartels where law and enforcement permit (Ch. 10, §10.2).

[AE] The prisoner’s-dilemma framework shows why firms can collectively prefer high prices yet individually have an incentive to cheat on a collusive agreement. Repeated interaction, monitoring, and punishment can support coordination, but the same forces do not guarantee stable cooperation (Ch. 10, §10.2).

[AR][BT] The source quotes Adam Smith’s warning that meetings among people in the same trade can end in “a conspiracy against the public” or a contrivance to raise prices, using the passage to bridge modern oligopoly analysis with an early account of collusion (Ch. 10, §10.2).

## Part IV: Microeconomic Policy Issues

### Chapter 11 — Monopoly and Antitrust Policy

[AP] Mergers can reduce costs, combine complementary capabilities, improve products, or extend economies of scale, but they can also lessen competition. Antitrust analysis therefore examines likely competitive effects rather than treating every merger as harmful (Ch. 11, §11.1).

[AP] Market definition matters because concentration depends on which products and geographic areas count as relevant substitutes. Concentration ratios and the Herfindahl-Hirschman Index summarise market shares, but neither mechanically resolves questions about entry, innovation, or competitive pressure (Ch. 11, §11.1).

[AP] Antitrust policy addresses collusion, predatory pricing, tying, bundling, exclusive dealing, and other restrictive practices when they maintain market power or impede competition. Conduct that looks similar can have different economic effects, requiring attention to context (Ch. 11, §11.2).

> “Under U.S. antitrust laws, monopoly itself is not illegal.”
> [V] (Ch. 11, §11.2)

[AP] A natural monopoly arises when economies of scale make one firm capable of supplying the entire market at lower average cost than several firms. Policy options include public ownership, cost-plus regulation, price-cap regulation, or allowing the firm to operate with oversight; each changes incentives for cost control, investment, quality, and regulatory gaming (Ch. 11, §11.3).

[AP] Deregulation can benefit consumers where technological and market changes have made competition feasible, but it can also expose weaknesses in transition design. Regulatory capture remains a risk when regulated firms possess concentrated information and incentives while consumer interests are diffuse (Ch. 11, §11.4).

[AE][BT] The source uses telecommunications, airlines, trucking, energy, and the Microsoft antitrust litigation to show that the appropriate policy depends on technology, market boundaries, network structure, and the conduct at issue (Ch. 11).

### Chapter 12 — Environmental Protection and Negative Externalities

[AP] A negative externality exists when production or consumption imposes costs on third parties that market participants do not fully bear. The market supply curve then reflects private marginal cost rather than the higher social marginal cost, producing more pollution-intensive output than the socially efficient quantity (Ch. 12, §12.1).

[AP] Command-and-control regulation mandates permissible technologies or emission levels. It can achieve direct reductions but often treats heterogeneous polluters uniformly, gives limited reward for exceeding the standard, and may fail to find the least-cost combination of abatement (Ch. 12, §12.2).

[AP] Market-oriented tools include pollution taxes, tradable permits, and well-defined property rights. They make pollution costly at the margin and allow firms with lower abatement costs to reduce more, helping attain an environmental target at lower total cost (Ch. 12, §12.3).

[AR][BT] The chapter presents the Coase theorem as the proposition that, with clearly assigned property rights and sufficiently low transaction costs, affected parties can bargain towards an efficient outcome. It also explains why numerous parties, uncertain damages, strategic behaviour, and enforcement costs limit this route in many environmental disputes (Ch. 12, §12.3).

[AP] Environmental policy should compare marginal benefits from cleaner air, water, health, and ecosystems with marginal abatement costs. The efficient point is not necessarily zero pollution, because eliminating the last units may require sacrificing outputs whose benefits exceed the additional environmental gain (Ch. 12, §§12.4, 12.6).

[AP][BT] The source reports substantial reductions in major U.S. air pollutants and notes that carbon dioxide emissions from coal consumption fell by about 66% between 1990 and 2023, while using Environmental Protection Agency and Energy Information Administration material to connect the model to observed trends (Ch. 12, §12.4).

[AP] Pollution that crosses borders or affects the global climate creates an international externality. Individual countries can free-ride on others’ abatement, making treaties, monitoring, burden sharing, and technology transfer part of the economic problem (Ch. 12, §12.5).

### Chapter 13 — Positive Externalities and Public Goods

[AP] Innovation produces private returns for inventors and spillover benefits for other firms and consumers. Because knowledge can be difficult to exclude and can often be reused without exhaustion, private markets may invest less in research and development than is socially desirable (Ch. 13, §13.1).

[AP] Policy responses include patents, direct public research, research grants, tax credits, education, and support for collaboration. Patents strengthen appropriability but restrict diffusion during their term; direct funding requires public selection of projects; tax incentives can support decentralised choices but may subsidise research firms would have undertaken anyway (Ch. 13, §13.2).

[AR][BT] The source reports Mariana Mazzucato and Carlota Perez’s account of public investment in foundational technologies and links it to cases such as computing, the internet, biotechnology, and GPS. The bridge supports a view of innovation as an ecosystem of public and private contributions rather than a simple opposition between them (Ch. 13, §§13.1–13.2).

> “A public good has two key characteristics: it is nonexcludable and non-rival.”
> [V] (Ch. 13, §13.3)

[AP] Nonexcludability creates a free-rider problem because people can benefit without paying; non-rivalry means one person’s use need not reduce availability to others. National defence and basic knowledge approximate public goods, while many actual goods combine public and private characteristics (Ch. 13, §13.3).

[AP] Common resources are rival but difficult to exclude, creating incentives for overuse. Public goods tend towards under-provision; common resources tend towards over-consumption (Ch. 13, §13.3).

[AR][BT] Garrett Hardin’s “tragedy of the commons” is presented as one account of resource depletion, while Elinor Ostrom’s work supplies evidence that communities can sometimes develop durable rules, monitoring, and sanctions to govern shared resources without either pure privatisation or central control (Ch. 13, §13.3).

### Chapter 14 — Labor Markets and Income

[AP] A profit-maximising firm’s demand for labour depends on the value of workers’ marginal product. In a competitive product market this is marginal product multiplied by product price; where the firm has product-market power, marginal revenue product uses marginal revenue instead (Ch. 14, §14.1).

[AP] The firm hires labour until the additional revenue generated by the last worker equals the marginal cost of employing that worker. Labour demand shifts with productivity, technology, output prices, complementary inputs, and product demand (Ch. 14, §14.1).

[AP] Monopsony gives a buyer of labour wage-setting power. Because hiring additional workers can require a higher wage, the marginal cost of labour can exceed the wage itself, producing lower employment and wages than in a competitive labour market (Ch. 14, §14.2).

[AP] Unions exercise market power on the supply side through collective bargaining. They may raise compensation, improve conditions, communicate worker information, and reduce turnover; higher negotiated labour costs can also alter employment, prices, investment, or substitution towards other inputs (Ch. 14, §14.3).

[AP] When a union faces a monopsonistic employer, bilateral monopoly makes the outcome depend on bargaining power and institutions rather than a unique competitive equilibrium. A wage increase can sometimes raise both pay and employment by counteracting monopsony power (Ch. 14, §14.3).

[AP] Human-capital differences, occupational choices, experience, hours, and job characteristics can explain portions of group earnings gaps, but they do not establish that the remainder is discrimination-free. The source distinguishes statistical decomposition from direct evidence such as matched audits and field experiments (Ch. 14, §14.4).

[AR][BT] Gary Becker is named in connection with a taste-based theory of discrimination, while William Darity Jr. is cited on discriminatory codes and institutional practices. The chapter treats discrimination as capable of persisting through employer, employee, customer, network, and institutional mechanisms (Ch. 14, §14.4).

[AP] Immigration expands labour supply but also adds consumers, entrepreneurs, taxpayers, and workers with complementary skills. Wage and employment effects therefore vary across groups, regions, time horizons, and the substitutability of immigrant and existing labour (Ch. 14, §14.5).

### Chapter 15 — Poverty and Economic Inequality

[AP] The U.S. poverty line originated from Mollie Orshansky’s food-budget method and is updated for inflation. It is an absolute threshold rather than a measure of relative position, and it does not by itself capture geographic cost differences, in-kind benefits, taxes, wealth, or temporary income changes (Ch. 15, §15.1).

[AP][BT] Census data cited by the source place the official U.S. poverty rate at 11.4% in 2020, representing 37.2 million people. Poverty rates differ by age, household type, race and ethnicity, education, employment, and other circumstances (Ch. 15, §15.1).

[AP] A poverty trap occurs when additional earnings trigger lost benefits or higher taxes so rapidly that the effective return to work is low. Safety-net design therefore balances income support, administrative simplicity, fiscal cost, and incentives (Ch. 15, §15.2).

[AP] Major U.S. programmes discussed include Temporary Assistance for Needy Families, Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, Medicaid, the Earned Income Tax Credit, and other targeted assistance. Cash transfers, in-kind benefits, tax credits, work requirements, and time limits affect recipients differently (Ch. 15, §15.2).

[AP] Income inequality can be described with quintile shares and the Lorenz curve, while wealth inequality reflects accumulated assets and debts. Income mobility means the people occupying each rank can change, but mobility does not make the distribution at a given time irrelevant (Ch. 15, §15.3).

[AR][BT] The chapter uses the “winner-take-all” account associated with Robert Frank and Philip Cook to explain how technology and large markets can magnify rewards for small differences among top performers (Ch. 15, §15.3).

[AP] Redistribution can reduce hardship and widen access to education, health, and opportunity, yet high marginal tax rates or abrupt benefit withdrawal can weaken incentives. The source rejects a simple claim that equality and output must always move in opposite directions: some measures can improve both opportunity and productivity (Ch. 15, §15.4).

### Chapter 16 — Information, Risk, and Insurance

[AP] Imperfect information exists when buyers or sellers lack relevant knowledge; asymmetric information exists when one side knows more than the other. In “lemons” markets, uncertainty about quality can reduce what buyers will pay, driving high-quality products out and making pessimistic expectations self-reinforcing (Ch. 16, §16.1).

[AP] Market responses include warranties, guarantees, reputation, reviews, certification, occupational licensing, collateral, cosigners, and signalling. Each can communicate information, but each also has costs and may create barriers to entry or false confidence (Ch. 16, §16.1).

[AP] Insurance pools independent risks so that uncertain individual losses become more predictable in aggregate. Premiums must cover expected claims, administration, and the insurer’s required return; actuarially fair insurance covers expected claims alone (Ch. 16, §16.2).

[AP] Moral hazard occurs when insurance changes behaviour after coverage is obtained. Deductibles, copayments, coinsurance, exclusions, monitoring, and provider-network rules leave policyholders bearing part of the marginal cost and can reduce overuse, but they also reduce risk protection (Ch. 16, §16.2).

[AP] Adverse selection occurs when people expecting higher claims are more likely to purchase coverage. If insurers cannot distinguish risk, premiums can rise, healthier customers can leave, and the pool can deteriorate (Ch. 16, §16.2).

[AE] The chapter’s health-insurance examples compare fee-for-service arrangements, health maintenance organisations, deductibles, copayments, and coinsurance to show that every contract allocates risk and incentives differently (Ch. 16, §16.2).

[AP][BT] Government interventions include disclosure and fraud rules, licensing, deposit and pension insurance, unemployment and workers’ compensation insurance, and the Affordable Care Act. The source frames these as responses to information failures and pooling problems that can themselves create cost, compliance, and incentive tradeoffs (Ch. 16, §16.3).

### Chapter 17 — Financial Markets

[AP] Financial markets move funds from savers to borrowers and convert claims with different combinations of risk, return, maturity, and liquidity. Firms finance investment through retained earnings, bank loans, bonds, venture capital, and shares; each distributes control, repayment obligations, and risk differently (Ch. 17, §17.1).

[AP] Bonds promise specified payments, while shares give residual ownership and may pay dividends or capital gains. Bondholders generally have priority over shareholders in bankruptcy, but default and interest-rate risk remain (Ch. 17, §17.1).

[AP] A higher expected return usually requires accepting greater risk, lower liquidity, or both. Bank deposits offer high liquidity and relatively low risk but correspondingly low returns; longer-term or lower-quality claims must generally offer more (Ch. 17, §17.2).

> “The bottom line on bank accounts looks like this: low risk means low rate of return but high liquidity.”
> [V] (Ch. 17, §17.2)

[AP] Diversification reduces exposure to firm-specific risk by combining assets whose returns do not move identically. It cannot eliminate economy-wide risk, and diversification benefits diminish when asset returns become highly correlated during crises (Ch. 17, §17.3).

[AP] Compound interest makes time a central determinant of accumulated wealth. Regular saving begun earlier can exceed larger contributions begun later because returns themselves earn returns (Ch. 17, §17.3).

[AR] The random-walk account holds that publicly known information is rapidly incorporated into traded prices, making persistent market outperformance difficult. The source does not claim prices are always correct; bubbles, crashes, insider information, and behavioural biases remain relevant qualifications (Ch. 17, §17.4).

### Chapter 18 — Public Economy

[AP] Public-choice analysis applies assumptions about incentives and limited information to voters, politicians, regulators, and interest groups. It asks how political institutions aggregate preferences rather than presuming that government automatically identifies and implements a unitary public interest (Ch. 18, §18.1).

[AP] Rational ignorance arises when becoming fully informed is costly while one person’s probability of changing an election is small. Low information can increase the influence of campaign messaging, party labels, organised groups, and visible but incomplete indicators (Ch. 18, §18.1).

[AR][BT] Anthony Downs is linked to the economic theory of democracy and the median-voter model, under which vote-seeking candidates in a one-dimensional majority contest have incentives to move towards the median preference (Ch. 18, §§18.1, 18.3).

[AR][BT] Mancur Olson’s collective-action analysis explains why small groups with concentrated stakes may organise more effectively than large groups whose individual stakes are small. The result can be policies with concentrated benefits and diffuse costs (Ch. 18, §18.2).

[AP] Regulatory capture, pork-barrel spending, logrolling, and special-interest legislation illustrate ways political incentives can diverge from aggregate welfare. Voting cycles also show that majority rule can fail to yield a stable ordering when preferences have certain configurations (Ch. 18, §§18.2–18.3).

[AP] Democratic institutions can nevertheless expose errors, permit opposition, disperse power, and replace decision-makers. The chapter’s conclusion is comparative: analyse the actual strengths and weaknesses of markets and governments rather than idealising one and demonising the other (Ch. 18, §18.3).

## Part V: The Macroeconomic Perspective and Goals

### Chapter 19 — The Macroeconomic Perspective

[AP] Gross domestic product is the market value of final goods and services produced within a country during a specified period. Counting final output avoids double counting intermediate inputs; production, expenditure, and income approaches should converge because one person’s expenditure becomes another’s revenue or income (Ch. 19, §§19.1–19.2).

[AP] The expenditure identity is `GDP = C + I + G + (X − M)`: household consumption, investment, government purchases, and net exports. Imports are subtracted not because they are intrinsically harmful but because they may already be included in consumption, investment, or government spending and were not domestically produced (Ch. 19, §19.2).

[AP] GDP excludes many household activities, informal and underground production, leisure, distributional information, environmental depletion, and changes in product quality that are difficult to price. It records production, not a complete account of welfare (Ch. 19, §§19.1, 19.4).

[AR][BT] The source notes Simon Kuznets’s role in developing national-income accounting (Ch. 19, §19.1).

[AP] Nominal GDP values current output at current prices; real GDP holds prices constant to isolate changes in production. The GDP deflator measures the associated economy-wide price change (Ch. 19, §19.3).

[AP] Peaks, recessions, troughs, and expansions describe the business cycle. GDP per capita supports comparisons of average material output, while purchasing-power adjustments improve cross-country comparison when price levels differ (Ch. 19, §§19.3–19.4).

> “No single number can capture all the elements of a term as broad as ‘standard of living.’”
> [V] (Ch. 19, §19.4)

### Chapter 20 — Economic Growth

> “Nothing is more important for people’s standard of living than sustained economic growth.”
> [V] (Ch. 20, §20.1)

[AP] Modern economic growth emerged after long periods in which living standards changed slowly. Even small differences in annual growth compound into large differences in output per person over generations (Ch. 20, §20.1).

[AP] Labour productivity—output per hour worked—is the immediate source of long-run growth in living standards. Its determinants include physical capital per worker, human capital, technology, infrastructure, institutions, and economies of scale (Ch. 20, §20.2).

[AP] An aggregate production function relates total output to labour, capital, and technology. Growth accounting attributes output growth to measured input growth and a residual commonly associated with technological and organisational progress (Ch. 20, §§20.2–20.3).

[AP] Capital deepening raises productivity, but diminishing returns mean that adding more capital to an unchanged workforce and technology eventually yields smaller gains. Sustained growth therefore depends heavily on technological change, skills, organisational knowledge, and institutions that support investment and innovation (Ch. 20, §20.3).

[AP] Rule of law, property and contractual rights, political stability, competitive markets, education, health, and openness to ideas can support growth. The text treats these as enabling conditions, not as a formula guaranteeing identical outcomes in every country (Ch. 20, §§20.1, 20.4).

[AR][BT] The chapter draws on Angus Maddison and Jan Luiten van Zanden for long-run historical comparisons, Robert Lucas for the scale of cross-country growth questions, Amartya Sen for the relationship between entitlements and famine, and Richard Easterlin for broader measures of living standards (Ch. 20).

[AP] Convergence can occur because lower-income economies can adopt existing technologies and because capital has higher marginal returns where it is scarce. It is conditional rather than automatic: conflict, weak institutions, poor health and education, low saving, or exclusion from trade and knowledge can obstruct catch-up (Ch. 20, §20.4).

### Chapter 21 — Unemployment

[AP] The labour force consists of people who are employed or unemployed and actively seeking work. The unemployment rate divides unemployed people by the labour force, while the labour-force participation rate divides the labour force by the relevant adult population (Ch. 21, §21.1).

[AP] People without work who have stopped searching are outside the official labour force, including discouraged workers. Underemployment and involuntary part-time work further show why one headline rate cannot capture every form of unused labour (Ch. 21, §21.1).

[BT] The source relies on the Bureau of Labor Statistics Current Population Survey and related measures to distinguish employment status, participation, and alternative unemployment indicators (Ch. 21, §21.1).

[AP] Unemployment differs across demographic groups and over the business cycle. Aggregate comparisons must account for changes in age structure, education, labour-force attachment, and other compositional factors (Ch. 21, §21.2).

[AP] Cyclical unemployment arises from deficient aggregate demand during downturns. Frictional unemployment arises while workers and employers search for suitable matches; structural unemployment arises when skills, locations, or wage expectations do not align with available jobs. The natural rate combines frictional and structural unemployment rather than implying zero unemployment (Ch. 21, §21.3).

[AP] Sticky-wage explanations include implicit contracts, efficiency wages, adverse selection from wage cuts, insider-outsider dynamics, and coordination problems. These mechanisms explain why wages may not fall rapidly enough to clear labour markets during a downturn (Ch. 21, §21.3).

[AP] Policies can support search, mobility, retraining, education, macroeconomic demand, and labour-market information. Their evaluation must include fiscal cost, job-match quality, incentives, distribution, and the distinction between cyclical and structural causes (Ch. 21, §21.4).

### Chapter 22 — Inflation

> “Inflation is a general and ongoing rise in the level of prices in an entire economy.”
> [V] (Ch. 22, §22.1)

[AP] Inflation is not merely a rise in one price. A price index values a representative basket, assigns a base-year value, and measures changes in the overall cost of that basket. The inflation rate is the percentage change in the index (Ch. 22, §22.1).

[AP] The Consumer Price Index follows household purchases; the Producer Price Index tracks prices received by producers; the GDP deflator covers domestically produced final output. Core measures remove volatile categories to identify persistent movement, but no measure is best for every purpose (Ch. 22, §§22.1–22.2).

[AP] Fixed baskets create substitution bias because consumers change what they buy as relative prices change. Quality and new-goods bias arise because products improve and entirely new choices appear. Statistical agencies adjust methods, but measurement remains approximate (Ch. 22, §22.2).

[AP] Deflation is a sustained decline in the overall price level; hyperinflation is extraordinarily rapid inflation. Unexpected inflation redistributes purchasing power between borrowers and lenders and between parties whose payments adjust at different speeds (Ch. 22, §§22.3–22.4).

[AP] Inflation creates costs through arbitrary redistribution, distorted price signals, tax interactions, planning difficulty, menu costs, and time spent avoiding depreciating money. Moderate predictable inflation is less disruptive than equally sized unexpected inflation because contracts and behaviour can adjust (Ch. 22, §22.4).

[AP] Indexation ties wages, pensions, taxes, or contracts to a price index. It can protect real purchasing power but may also propagate inflation and cannot perfectly match every household’s cost of living (Ch. 22, §22.5).

### Chapter 23 — The International Trade and Capital Flows

[AP] The current account includes trade in goods and services, cross-border income, and unilateral transfers. The capital and financial side records purchases and sales of assets. Accounting requires a current-account deficit to be matched by a net financial inflow and a surplus by a net outflow (Ch. 23, §§23.1–23.2).

[AP] The Robinson–Friday example strips international exchange to two parties: if one receives more goods than it supplies, the difference must be financed by an asset or promise flowing the other way. The example makes the balance-of-payments identity concrete (Ch. 23, §23.1).

[AP] The national saving and investment identity links domestic investment to private saving, government saving, and foreign financial capital. A trade deficit can finance productive investment or current consumption; its implications depend on what attracts the funds and whether future income can service the resulting claims (Ch. 23, §23.3).

[AP] Trade deficits are not inherently proof of economic weakness, nor are surpluses inherently proof of strength. Fast growth and attractive investment opportunities can draw capital in, while weak domestic demand can contribute to a surplus (Ch. 23, §23.4).

[AP] The level of trade measures how much a country exports and imports relative to its economy; the trade balance measures the difference between them. A country can have extensive two-way trade with a nearly balanced account or little trade with a sizeable proportional imbalance (Ch. 23, §23.5).

## Part VI: A Framework for Macroeconomic Analysis

### Chapter 24 — The Aggregate Demand/Aggregate Supply Model

[AP] Aggregate demand represents total planned spending on domestic output at different price levels. It slopes downward through wealth effects, interest-rate effects, and changes in the relative price of domestic and foreign goods—not because the microeconomic law of demand can simply be transferred to the entire economy (Ch. 24, §24.1).

[AP] Aggregate demand shifts when consumption, investment, government spending, exports, or imports change for reasons other than the current price level. Confidence, wealth, taxes, interest rates, foreign growth, and exchange rates are among the determinants (Ch. 24, §24.2).

[AP] Short-run aggregate supply slopes upward because some wages and input prices adjust slowly. Long-run aggregate supply is vertical at potential GDP, which depends on labour, capital, technology, and institutions (Ch. 24, §24.3).

[AP] A rightward AD shift can raise output and employment when substantial slack exists but produces more inflation as the economy approaches capacity. An adverse aggregate-supply shift can simultaneously reduce output and raise prices, generating stagflation (Ch. 24, §§24.3–24.4).

[AE] COVID-19 is treated as both an aggregate-supply shock—through closures, disrupted production, and supply chains—and an aggregate-demand shock through income loss, uncertainty, and reduced spending in affected services (Ch. 24, §24.4).

[AR][BT] The source associates Say’s law with Jean-Baptiste Say and the long-run claim that supply generates purchasing power, while Keynes’s law expresses the short-run possibility that demand determines realised output. Its synthesis maps the Keynesian, intermediate, and neoclassical zones onto one SRAS curve (Ch. 24, §§24.4–24.5).

> “Demand creates its own supply.”
> [V] (Ch. 24, §24.5)

### Chapter 25 — The Keynesian Perspective

[AP] Keynesian analysis begins from the possibility that aggregate expenditure can remain too low to purchase potential output. Firms respond to weak sales by reducing production and employment, so an economy need not quickly self-correct to full employment (Ch. 25, §25.1).

[AP] Consumption depends heavily on disposable income and wealth; investment depends on expected profitability, interest rates, technology, and confidence; government spending is set politically; net exports depend on foreign income, domestic income, relative prices, and exchange rates (Ch. 25, §25.2).

[AP] Sticky wages and prices prevent rapid market clearing. Explanations include contracts, morale and productivity effects, menu costs, imperfect information, and coordination failures. A firm that cuts wages or prices may harm itself if other firms and incomes do not adjust simultaneously (Ch. 25, §25.3).

[AP] The spending multiplier arises because one person’s expenditure becomes another’s income, inducing further consumption. Leakages into saving, taxes, and imports reduce the multiplier, and capacity constraints make its price and output effects depend on the economy’s position relative to potential GDP (Ch. 25, §25.4; App. D).

[AR][BT] A. W. Phillips is named in connection with the observed short-run inverse relationship between wage inflation and unemployment. The chapter’s modern Phillips curve adds expected inflation and supply shocks, so the curve can shift and does not represent a permanent menu of choices (Ch. 25, §25.5).

[AP] Expansionary fiscal and monetary policy can raise aggregate demand in a recessionary gap; contractionary policy can restrain an inflationary gap. The Keynesian prescription is aggregate stabilisation, not detailed government direction of every price and quantity (Ch. 25, §25.6).

### Chapter 26 — The Neoclassical Perspective

[AP] The neoclassical perspective places potential GDP and long-run aggregate supply at the centre of analysis. Flexible prices and wages eventually return output to its productive capacity, so long-run changes in aggregate demand primarily affect the price level (Ch. 26, §26.1).

[AP] Rational expectations use available information and an understanding of policy, while adaptive expectations extrapolate from past experience. Expectations can speed adjustment and weaken predictable policy effects, but information is costly and forecasts remain imperfect (Ch. 26, §26.2).

[AP] The text estimates that the transition from short-run Keynesian conditions to longer-run neoclassical adjustment may take roughly two to five years, while stressing that timing varies with the shock, institutions, and expectations (Ch. 26, §26.3).

[AR][BT] Milton Friedman is quoted for the distinction between a temporary inflation–unemployment tradeoff and the absence of a permanent tradeoff. In the long run, attempts to hold unemployment below its natural rate raise expected and actual inflation rather than permanently increasing employment (Ch. 26, §26.3).

[AP] Neoclassical policy priorities include credible low inflation, flexible labour and product markets, competition, saving and investment, education, research, infrastructure, and institutional conditions that increase productivity and potential output (Ch. 26, §26.4).

[AR][BT] Robert Solow is used to resist an artificial choice between schools: short-run Keynesian stabilisation and long-run neoclassical growth analysis answer different questions. The source’s final synthesis assigns greater Keynesian relevance to recession and adjustment periods and greater neoclassical relevance to long-run capacity (Ch. 26, §26.5).

## Part VII: Monetary and Fiscal Policy

### Chapter 27 — Money and Banking

[AP] Money serves as a medium of exchange, a store of value, a unit of account, and a standard of deferred payment. It reduces the barter requirement for a double coincidence of wants and supports specialisation and complex exchange (Ch. 27, §27.1).

[AP] Commodity money has nonmonetary value, commodity-backed money is redeemable for a specified commodity, and fiat money is accepted because law, convention, and confidence support it rather than because the object itself has equivalent commodity value (Ch. 27, §27.1).

[AP] M1 comprises the most liquid spendable balances, while M2 adds less immediately spendable forms. The source explains that the Federal Reserve’s 2020 reclassification of savings deposits altered the reported aggregates, making historical comparisons across the definition change hazardous (Ch. 27, §27.2).

[AP] Banks provide payment services and act as financial intermediaries. On a bank balance sheet, loans, bonds, and reserves are assets; deposits and borrowing are liabilities; net worth or bank capital is the difference (Ch. 27, §27.3).

[AP] Securitisation pools loans and sells claims on their cash flows. It can diversify and distribute risk, but weak underwriting, opaque structures, maturity mismatch, and leverage can transmit losses through the financial system (Ch. 27, §27.3).

[AE] The Safe and Secure Bank and related T-account examples trace how deposits, reserves, loans, and net worth change after transactions. The exercises show that a loan creates a deposit and that repayment destroys deposit money, subject to capital, reserve, risk, and demand constraints (Ch. 27, §27.4; App. E).

[AP] The simple money-multiplier formula illustrates repeated lending under a fixed reserve ratio, but the source cautions against treating it as a mechanical description of modern banking. Banks may hold excess reserves, borrowers may not demand loans, currency may leave the banking system, and the ample-reserves framework changes the operating environment (Ch. 27, §27.4).

> “Money and banks are marvelous social inventions that help a modern economy to function.”
> [V] (Ch. 27, §27.5)

[AP] Cryptocurrencies can transfer value without a conventional bank ledger, but their price volatility, transaction capacity, regulation, security, and acceptance affect whether they perform the standard functions of money (Ch. 27, §27.5).

### Chapter 28 — Monetary Policy and Bank Regulation

[AP] The Federal Reserve System combines a Board of Governors, twelve regional Federal Reserve Banks, and the Federal Open Market Committee. Its responsibilities include monetary policy, bank supervision, payment-system support, financial stability, and lender-of-last-resort functions (Ch. 28, §28.1).

[AP] Deposit insurance reduces incentives for bank runs by assuring depositors up to the statutory limit; the source gives the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation limit as $250,000 per depositor for covered accounts. Insurance can also create moral hazard, making supervision and capital requirements important complements (Ch. 28, §§28.1–28.2).

[AP] Under a limited-reserves framework, the traditional tools are open-market operations, reserve requirements, and the discount rate. Bond purchases add reserves and tend to lower interest rates; sales remove reserves and tend to raise them (Ch. 28, §28.3; App. E).

[AP] Under the modern ample-reserves framework, the interest rate on reserve balances and related administered rates help place a floor under overnight market rates. The federal funds rate remains the communicated target even though reserve quantities are no longer managed as if they were tightly scarce (Ch. 28, §28.3).

[AP] Expansionary monetary policy lowers targeted interest rates and supports borrowing, consumption, investment, and aggregate demand; contractionary policy does the reverse to restrain inflation. Exchange rates and asset prices provide additional transmission channels (Ch. 28, §28.4).

[AP] Quantitative easing purchases longer-term assets when short-term policy rates are near their lower bound. It aims to lower longer-term yields and improve financial conditions but raises questions about portfolio risk, market functioning, distribution, and exit strategy (Ch. 28, §28.4).

[AR][BT] Milton Friedman is quoted for the proposition that monetary policy can prevent money itself from becoming a major source of economic disturbance. The source uses the Great Depression and later crises to connect central-bank action with the dangers of monetary contraction and financial panic (Ch. 28, §28.5).

[AP] Policy limitations include recognition and transmission lags, uncertain velocity, banks’ willingness to lend, borrowers’ willingness to borrow, asset bubbles, leverage, and the difficulty of stimulating demand by lowering rates once they are already very low (Ch. 28, §28.5).

### Chapter 29 — Exchange Rates and International Capital Flows

[AP] The foreign-exchange market trades currencies. Demand for a currency arises from foreigners buying its exports and assets; supply arises when domestic residents buy foreign goods, services, and assets. The equilibrium exchange rate equates these flows (Ch. 29, §29.1).

[AP] Appreciation makes a currency more valuable relative to another: imports become cheaper to domestic buyers while exports become more expensive to foreigners. Depreciation reverses these effects. Neither movement benefits everyone within the economy (Ch. 29, §29.1).

> “Stronger currency is not necessarily better, it is just different.”
> [V] (Ch. 29, §29.1)

[AP] Expected returns, interest rates, inflation, productivity, trade prospects, political risk, and expectations shift currency demand and supply. Because financial transactions are large and rapid, anticipated future policy can affect an exchange rate before trade quantities respond (Ch. 29, §29.2).

[AP] Purchasing-power parity argues that arbitrage tends to align prices of tradable goods after currency conversion. Transport costs, taxes, nontradable services, product differences, market power, and slow adjustment explain persistent departures (Ch. 29, §29.3).

[AP] Exchange-rate changes influence aggregate demand through net exports and aggregate supply through imported input costs. Banks and firms that borrow in foreign currency but earn in domestic currency can face a destructive balance-sheet mismatch after depreciation (Ch. 29, §29.4).

[AP] Exchange-rate regimes range from floating rates to soft pegs, hard pegs, dollarisation, and merged currencies. Greater stability can support trade and investment, but maintaining a peg can sacrifice monetary-policy autonomy and require large reserves or painful domestic adjustment (Ch. 29, §29.5).

[AP][BT] James Tobin’s proposed tax on short-term currency transactions is discussed as a possible way to discourage destabilising flows, with practical concerns about avoidance, international coordination, and the distinction between speculation and useful liquidity (Ch. 29, §29.5).

### Chapter 30 — Government Budgets and Fiscal Policy

[AP] A budget deficit occurs when government spending exceeds tax revenue during a period; a surplus occurs when revenue exceeds spending. The national debt is the accumulated stock of past borrowing, adjusted for repayments (Ch. 30, §30.1).

> “The deficit is not the debt.”
> [V] (Ch. 30, §30.1)

[AP] Governments finance deficits by issuing Treasury securities. Debt sustainability depends not only on its nominal size but on interest rates, maturity, currency, growth, revenue capacity, investor confidence, and the debt-to-GDP ratio (Ch. 30, §30.1).

[AP] Taxes may be progressive, proportional, or regressive relative to income. Statutory rates differ from effective rates, and the economic burden can be shifted through prices, wages, returns, and behavioural responses (Ch. 30, §30.2).

[AP] Expansionary fiscal policy increases government spending or reduces taxes to shift aggregate demand right; contractionary policy reduces spending or raises taxes to shift it left. The appropriate direction depends on whether the economy faces a recessionary or inflationary gap (Ch. 30, §30.3).

[AP] Automatic stabilisers—such as progressive income taxes and unemployment-related benefits—change with economic conditions without new legislation. A standardised employment budget attempts to separate cyclical changes in the deficit from deliberate policy (Ch. 30, §30.4).

[AP] Discretionary fiscal policy faces recognition, legislative, implementation, and impact lags. Temporary measures may be saved rather than spent, politically attractive programmes may persist after the recession, and public borrowing can crowd out private investment (Ch. 30, §30.5).

[AP] A constitutional or statutory balanced-budget rule could restrain chronic deficits but would force tax increases or spending cuts during recessions unless it allowed exceptions. It would also reduce the operation of automatic stabilisers (Ch. 30, §30.6).

### Chapter 31 — The Impacts of Government Borrowing

[AP] The national saving and investment identity makes the financing constraint explicit. When government borrowing rises, some combination of private saving, private investment, and foreign financial inflows must adjust (Ch. 31, §31.1).

[AP] If domestic saving does not rise, a budget deficit can raise interest rates and crowd out private physical capital. If foreign funds enter instead, the currency can appreciate and the trade deficit can widen. Outcomes depend on capital mobility, monetary conditions, confidence, and the economy’s initial slack (Ch. 31, §§31.1–31.2).

[AP] Budget and trade deficits are related through the saving identity, but they need not move one-for-one. Private saving and investment can change independently, so the source rejects a mechanically deterministic “twin deficits” relationship (Ch. 31, §31.2).

[AR][BT] Ricardian equivalence is presented as the argument that households anticipating future taxes save an amount equal to current deficit-financed tax relief. The source reports empirical estimates suggesting only partial offsets—around 30 cents of extra saving per dollar of deficit in one cited line of research—rather than full equivalence (Ch. 31, §31.3).

[AP] Government borrowing can reduce future living standards when it finances current consumption and displaces productive capital. Borrowing for infrastructure, education, health, or research can instead raise future productivity if project benefits exceed financing and opportunity costs (Ch. 31, §31.4).

[AP] Large and persistent deficits can raise interest burdens, limit future fiscal flexibility, increase exposure to interest-rate or confidence shocks, and create intergenerational transfers. These risks depend on the use of funds and economic context, not on a claim that every deficit is equally harmful (Ch. 31, §31.4).

## Part VIII: International Economics

### Chapter 32 — Macroeconomic Policy Around the World

[AP] National averages conceal enormous differences in population, income, institutions, structure, and distribution. GDP per capita is more useful than total GDP for comparing average production, but regional aggregates can still hide major variation among member countries (Ch. 32, §32.1).

[AP][BT] The World Bank’s income classifications organise economies into income groups using gross national income per person. The text treats these as descriptive categories whose thresholds and memberships change rather than fixed stages every country follows identically (Ch. 32, §32.1).

[AP] High-income economies emphasise innovation, productivity, ageing populations, fiscal sustainability, and maintenance of complex institutions. Middle-income economies often face the challenge of moving beyond low-cost production towards skills, capital deepening, and innovation. Low-income economies face more acute constraints in health, education, infrastructure, governance, finance, and basic security (Ch. 32, §§32.2–32.4).

[AP] A poverty trap can arise when low income prevents adequate saving, education, health, and infrastructure, which in turn keeps productivity and income low. Foreign aid, debt relief, microfinance, public health, education, trade access, and institutional reform are proposed responses, each with implementation and incentive risks (Ch. 32, §32.4).

[AR][BT] Abhijit Banerjee and Esther Duflo are connected to evidence-based interventions in *Poor Economics*. Dambisa Moyo’s *Dead Aid* and William Easterly’s work are reported as critiques of aid that weakens accountability or misunderstands local incentives (Ch. 32, §32.4).

[AR][BT] The Lewis dual-sector model describes development as labour moving from low-productivity subsistence activity towards higher-productivity modern production. The source uses it as a framework, while recognising that urban unemployment, informality, skills, and institutional barriers complicate the transition (Ch. 32, §32.3).

[AP] Macroeconomic problems take different forms across income groups. High unemployment can be cyclical, structural, or partly a measurement issue in subsistence economies; inflation can reflect monetary financing of deficits; and trade or capital-flow imbalances can expose small banking systems to sudden reversals (Ch. 32, §§32.2–32.4).

### Chapter 33 — International Trade

[AP] Absolute advantage means producing a good with fewer resources; comparative advantage means producing it at lower opportunity cost. Trade is governed by comparative rather than absolute advantage (Ch. 33, §§33.1–33.2).

[AE] The source’s two-country production examples calculate opportunity costs from labour requirements and production possibilities. They show that a country with an absolute advantage in both goods can specialise in the good where its relative advantage is greatest, while the less productive country specialises where its disadvantage is smallest (Ch. 33, §§33.1–33.2).

[AR][BT] David Ricardo’s 1817 account is explicitly connected to the comparative-advantage principle. The chapter translates the historical argument into production-possibility and opportunity-cost terms (Ch. 33, §33.1).

[AP] Specialisation and trade allow consumption beyond a country’s own production possibilities, provided the terms of trade lie between the countries’ opportunity costs. The gains are aggregate possibilities; they do not establish that every person within each country gains (Ch. 33, §33.2).

[AP] Intra-industry trade exchanges differentiated versions of similar products. It supports finer specialisation, learning, economies of scale, competition among large producers, and greater consumer variety even between economies with similar resource endowments (Ch. 33, §33.3).

[AP] Global value chains divide design, components, assembly, marketing, and support across countries. Comparative advantage can therefore attach to stages and organisational capabilities rather than to an entire finished product (Ch. 33, §33.4).

[AP] Comparative advantage can evolve with education, infrastructure, institutions, accumulated knowledge, innovation, and scale. The concept explains gains from differences but does not require those differences to be natural or permanent (Ch. 33, §33.4).

### Chapter 34 — Globalization and Protectionism

[AP] Protectionist instruments include tariffs, quotas, subsidies, local-content rules, product standards, administrative barriers, and anti-dumping measures. A tariff raises the domestic price, expands domestic production, contracts domestic consumption, reduces imports, transfers surplus, raises government revenue, and creates deadweight loss (Ch. 34, §34.1).

[AE] The U.S. sugar example applies demand and supply to import restrictions. Producers benefit from a higher domestic price, while consumers and sugar-using industries bear costs that exceed the gains to producers and government (Ch. 34, §34.1).

[AP] Protection can preserve jobs in the protected industry but reduce real wages through higher prices and destroy jobs in industries using the protected input or selling goods consumers can no longer afford. Counting only the visible protected jobs omits these indirect effects (Ch. 34, §34.2).

[AP] Trade raises average productivity and income by moving resources towards comparative advantage, but import-competing workers, firms, and communities can incur concentrated and persistent losses. Adjustment assistance, mobility support, education, wage insurance, and regional policy address different parts of this distributional problem (Ch. 34, §34.2).

[AP] Labour-standard objections must compare export employment with workers’ actual alternatives, not solely with high-income-country standards. At the same time, coercion, unsafe conditions, child labour, and weak bargaining power remain legitimate policy concerns (Ch. 34, §34.3).

[AP] Infant-industry protection argues that temporary support can help a sector reach scale and acquire capabilities. The source finds that such protection often becomes permanent and costly, while noting East Asian cases in which support was selective, export-disciplined, and tied to performance and termination rules (Ch. 34, §34.4).

[AP] Anti-dumping action responds to exports priced below a specified benchmark, but measuring “fair value” is difficult and the process can become ordinary protection under another label. Predatory dumping requires later monopoly pricing to recover initial losses, which may be difficult when entry and international supply remain available (Ch. 34, §34.4).

[AP] Environmental and safety standards can correct genuine cross-border harms, yet standards can also discriminate against imports. A policy aimed directly at the externality and applied equally to domestic and foreign producers is preferable to a broad tariff (Ch. 34, §34.5).

[AP] National-security arguments are strongest where dependence would create a concrete strategic vulnerability. Applied without limits, the same argument can be used for nearly any industry and may accelerate depletion of domestic resources by discouraging imports (Ch. 34, §34.5).

[AP][BT] The General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade and its successor, the World Trade Organization, provide rules and negotiations through which countries exchange market access and contest trade restrictions. Regional arrangements range from free-trade areas to common markets and economic unions (Ch. 34, §34.6).

[AP] International agreements can help governments resist concentrated domestic protectionist interests by making liberalisation reciprocal. They also constrain unilateral policy and can generate disputes over sovereignty, enforcement, and whose standards govern trade (Ch. 34, §34.6).

[AR][BT] The source uses Ambrose Bierce’s satirical definition of a tariff—designed to protect the domestic producer “against the greed of his consumer”—to expose the producer-centred logic of protection (Ch. 34, §34.1).

[AP] The chapter’s final position is to retain the gains from trade while addressing adjustment, distribution, labour, environmental, and security concerns with policies directed at those problems. Cutting off trade generally sacrifices broad gains without reliably solving the underlying concern (Ch. 34, §34.7).

## Appendices

### Appendix A — The Use of Mathematics in Principles of Economics

> “Economics is not math.”
> [V] (App. A)

[AP] Mathematics is presented as one language for expressing relationships, not the substance of economics itself. Equations, tables, and graphs clarify assumptions and make implications checkable, but historical, institutional, verbal, and empirical reasoning remain necessary (App. A).

[AP] The appendix covers variables, functions, linear equations, slopes, intercepts, percentage changes, compound growth, and line, bar, and pie graphs. It stresses reading axes, units, scales, and whether a graph shows levels, rates, shares, or changes (App. A).

[AP] Correlation in a graph does not by itself establish causation. Truncated axes, selective date ranges, unusual scales, omitted categories, and inappropriate averaging can alter visual impressions; the instruction is to interpret quantitative displays cautiously (App. A).

### Appendix B — Indifference Curves

[AP] An indifference curve joins consumption bundles yielding equal utility. Curves slope downward because maintaining utility requires compensating for less of one good with more of another, and curves farther from the origin represent greater attainable utility when both goods are desirable (App. B).

[AP] Diminishing marginal rate of substitution gives indifference curves their convex shape. The budget line gives feasible bundles, and an interior utility maximum occurs where the budget line is tangent to the highest attainable indifference curve (App. B).

[AP] Income changes shift the budget line in parallel; price changes rotate it. Comparing tangencies decomposes a price response into substitution and income effects (App. B).

[AP] The same framework analyses labour–leisure choice and intertemporal consumption. A wage or interest-rate change has opposing substitution and income effects, so the net response cannot always be signed from theory alone (App. B).

### Appendix C — Present Discounted Value

[AP] Present discounted value converts future payments into their value today using an opportunity interest rate. Payments farther in the future or discounted at a higher rate have a lower present value (App. C).

[AP] Bond and stock valuation apply the same principle to expected cash flows. Risk, uncertainty, maturity, and alternative returns affect the discount rate, while forecasts of dividends or resale values affect expected payments (App. C).

[AP] Discounting also applies to education, environmental policy, infrastructure, retirement, and other choices whose costs and benefits occur at different dates. The selected discount rate can materially change the apparent desirability of long-lived projects (App. C).

### Appendix D — The Expenditure-Output Model

[AP] The Keynesian cross compares aggregate expenditure with output. Equilibrium occurs where planned expenditure equals production; unintended inventory changes cause firms to adjust output when the two differ (App. D).

[AP] Consumption is modelled as autonomous consumption plus the marginal propensity to consume times disposable income. Investment, government purchases, exports, taxes, saving, and imports add injections or leakages to the expenditure process (App. D).

[AP] A recessionary gap occurs when equilibrium output is below potential GDP; an inflationary gap occurs when planned expenditure would push output beyond sustainable capacity. Fiscal changes can close either gap in the model (App. D).

[AP] The simple multiplier is larger when induced consumption is strong and smaller when saving, taxes, and imports absorb additional income. The model illustrates cumulative demand effects but abstracts from price changes, interest rates, financing, expectations, and capacity responses (App. D).

### Appendix E — The Expenditure-Output Model and the Open-Market-Operations Balance Sheet

[AP] The appendix traces open-market purchases and sales through central-bank and commercial-bank balance sheets under a limited-reserves framework. A central-bank bond purchase increases reserve balances and the seller’s deposit; a sale reverses those entries (App. E).

[AP] The accounting demonstrates how monetary policy changes the composition and quantity of financial assets held by banks and the public. It supplements rather than replaces the chapter’s distinction between limited- and ample-reserves operating frameworks (App. E; Ch. 28, §28.3).

## Recurring analytical architecture

### Scarcity, opportunity cost, and the margin

[AP] The same decision rule recurs at every scale: compare additional benefit with additional opportunity cost. Consumers allocate budgets by marginal utility per dollar; firms produce where marginal revenue equals marginal cost; employers hire until marginal revenue product equals marginal labour cost; pollution control continues while marginal environmental benefit exceeds marginal abatement cost; and governments compare the incremental stabilisation or growth benefit of policy with its fiscal and behavioural cost (Chs. 2, 6, 8–9, 12, 14, 30–31).

### Equilibrium and adjustment

[AP] Equilibrium is a consistency condition, not a moral endorsement. Demand-and-supply equilibrium clears a market; consumer equilibrium exhausts the feasible utility-improving reallocations; firm equilibrium maximises profit given price and cost; macroeconomic equilibrium aligns aggregate expenditure and output; foreign-exchange equilibrium aligns currency demand and supply; and balance-of-payments identities reconcile real and financial flows (Chs. 3, 6, 8–10, 23–25, 29; App. D).

[AP] Adjustment mechanisms differ in speed and reliability. Prices can transmit information quickly in some markets, while contracts, search, regulation, expectations, balance sheets, and coordination problems slow adjustment elsewhere. This difference underlies much of the contrast between competitive-market models and the Keynesian account of unemployment (Chs. 4, 8, 16–18, 21, 24–26).

### Efficiency and distribution

[AP] Productive efficiency asks whether output is produced at minimum resource cost; allocative efficiency asks whether the output mix corresponds to marginal social benefits and costs. Consumer and producer surplus measure gains from exchange, but neither alone answers who receives those gains or whether starting endowments are just (Chs. 2–3, 8–15).

[AP] Policies and market changes almost always redistribute as well as alter total surplus.
