Taxes burden buyers and sellers according to elasticities; inflation redistributes between parties to nominal contracts; exchange-rate changes divide importers from exporters; trade benefits expanding sectors while injuring import-competing ones; and environmental rules divide compliance costs from health and ecological benefits (Chs. 5, 12, 15, 22, 29, 33–34).

### Private and social incentives

[AP] Externalities, public goods, information problems, monopoly, and political collective action all arise from a gap between an actor’s private incentives and broader social effects. Corrective policy seeks to narrow that gap through prices, rights, information, rules, provision, or institutional design (Chs. 9–18).

[AP] The source applies the same scrutiny to intervention: a policy’s stated public purpose does not ensure efficient implementation. Regulators may be captured, programmes may create poverty traps, insurance may cause moral hazard, protection may become permanent, and fiscal or monetary action may arrive after conditions change (Chs. 11, 15–16, 18, 28, 30, 34).

### Stocks, flows, and accounting identities

[AP] The text repeatedly distinguishes stocks from flows: wealth from income, debt from deficit, capital from investment, money holdings from spending, and foreign asset positions from current trade. Confusing these categories produces false causal claims even when the arithmetic appears plausible (Chs. 17, 19, 23, 27, 30–31).

[AP] Accounting identities constrain possible stories without by themselves establishing behavioural causation. GDP’s expenditure identity, bank balance sheets, the quantity equation, the balance of payments, and the national saving-and-investment identity must hold, but theory and evidence are still required to determine which variable adjusted and why (Chs. 19, 23, 27–31).

### Short run and long run

[AP] Fixed inputs, sticky prices, incomplete adjustment, and existing contracts dominate many short-run questions. Entry and exit, capital adjustment, technological change, expectation revision, and institutional development matter more over longer periods (Chs. 7–8, 20–21, 24–26).

[AP] The distinction prevents policy conclusions from being transferred mechanically across horizons. Demand management can affect output and employment during a recession, while sustained long-run gains depend on productivity and potential output; protection can preserve a current industry while weakening future competition; and deficits can support demand now while displacing or financing capital later (Chs. 26, 30–34).

## Positions explicitly framed against

- **Economics as a doctrine supplying compulsory answers.** [AR][BT] Keynes’s “method rather than a doctrine” formulation and the text’s positive–normative distinction frame economics as a way to clarify consequences, not a substitute for social values (Chs. 1–2).
- **Choices without opportunity cost.** [V] “A fundamental principle of economics is that every choice has an opportunity cost.” (Ch. 2, §2.1).
- **Treating one side of a market as the sole determinant of price.** [AP][BT] The Marshall scissors analogy makes equilibrium jointly dependent on demand and supply (Ch. 3, §3.5).
- **Confusing a movement along a curve with a shift of the curve.** [AP] Own-price changes alter quantity demanded or supplied; other determinants shift the relationship (Ch. 3, §3.2).
- **Assuming the legal payer bears an entire tax.** [AP] Economic incidence depends on relative elasticities (Ch. 5, §5.3).
- **Treating accounting profit as economic profit.** [AP] Implicit opportunity costs distinguish the two (Ch. 7, §7.1).
- **Equating zero economic profit with no return.** [AP] Normal compensation for all opportunity costs is included in economic cost (Ch. 8, §8.3).
- **Judging monopoly solely by high prices.** [AP] The efficiency loss arises from restricted output and the resulting unrealised gains from trade (Ch. 9, §9.2).
- **Treating monopoly status itself as automatically illegal.** [V] “Under U.S. antitrust laws, monopoly itself is not illegal.” (Ch. 11, §11.2).
- **Assuming zero pollution is automatically efficient.** [AP] Environmental policy compares marginal social benefits and costs (Ch. 12, §12.6).
- **Assuming public goods will be adequately financed through voluntary individual payment.** [AP] Nonexcludability creates incentives to free-ride (Ch. 13, §13.3).
- **Inferring an absence of discrimination from explained wage differences.** [AP] Human-capital controls and direct evidence answer different questions (Ch. 14, §14.4).
- **Designing safety-net policy without marginal incentives.** [AP] Benefit withdrawal and taxes can create a poverty trap (Ch. 15, §15.2).
- **Assuming insurance can remove risk without changing behaviour or selection.** [AP] Moral hazard and adverse selection shape viable contracts (Ch. 16, §16.2).
- **Idealising either markets or government.** [AP] The text calls for comparison of real institutional strengths and failures (Ch. 18, §18.3).
- **Equating GDP with welfare.** [V] “No single number can capture all the elements of a term as broad as ‘standard of living.’” (Ch. 19, §19.4).
- **Equating the unemployment rate with every form of unused labour.** [AP] Participation, discouraged workers, and underemployment require separate measures (Ch. 21, §21.1).
- **Calling any individual price rise inflation.** [V] Inflation is “a general and ongoing rise in the level of prices in an entire economy.” (Ch. 22, §22.1).
- **Treating a trade deficit as intrinsically bad or a surplus as intrinsically good.** [AP] Each is the counterpart of financial flows whose effect depends on their causes and uses (Ch. 23, §§23.3–23.4).
- **Forcing Keynesian and neoclassical analysis into one exclusive horizon.** [AP] The source assigns them different short- and long-run domains of greatest relevance (Ch. 26, §26.5).
- **Applying the simple money multiplier mechanically to modern banking.** [AP] Loan demand, capital, risk, excess reserves, currency holdings, and the ample-reserves framework interrupt the textbook chain (Ch. 27, §27.4).
- **Assuming a stronger currency is unambiguously better.** [V] “Stronger currency is not necessarily better, it is just different.” (Ch. 29, §29.1).
- **Confusing a flow deficit with the stock of debt.** [V] “The deficit is not the debt.” (Ch. 30, §30.1).
- **Treating budget and trade deficits as mechanically identical twins.** [AP] Private saving and investment also adjust within the national identity (Ch. 31, §31.2).
- **Equating absolute advantage with the basis for trade.** [AP] Comparative opportunity cost governs specialisation and mutual gain (Ch. 33, §§33.1–33.2).
- **Counting protected jobs without the wider employment and consumer effects of protection.** [AP] Higher input and consumer prices shift losses to other industries and households (Ch. 34, §34.2).
- **Assuming a tariff is the best remedy for a labour, safety, environmental, or adjustment problem.** [AP] Policies aimed directly at the underlying failure are generally more precise (Ch. 34, §§34.3–34.7).
- **Treating mathematics as economics itself.** [V] “Economics is not math.” (App. A).
